- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly, especially after spikes.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.50), model often underestimates; adjust upward, particularly if recent price is falling sharply.
- Model frequently overreacts to short-term sentiment swings — if sentiment shifts sharply, reduce forecast magnitude by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.
- After a price spike, model often continues upward; if sentiment turns negative or neutral, apply mean reversion by lowering forecast 3–5% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
- If sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.00–0.33), model tends to overfit recent trends; use 3–5 day moving average or lagged 1–2 day price to anchor forecast.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture long-term mean reversion; if sentiment is weak or negative, apply downward bias of 2–5% to align with true outcome trend.
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative sentiment (e.g., 3+ consecutive negative values), model underestimates; increase forecast by 3–7% to counteract pessimism.
- If model forecast is > 10% above recent 18-day average, reduce by 5–10% if sentiment is neutral or negative — avoid overconfidence in upward momentum.
